newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian opposition fails to win political status.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian opposition fails to win political status.

text.p: Nigeria celebrates 36 years of independence on Tuesday with the registration of five political parties for future elections, but opponents of the military government are not among them.

The National Electoral Commission (NECON) set tough conditions for parties to win official registration and when it announced the successful five on Monday, they were all from the political centre ground.
"No political association that is critical of the military government appears to have been successful," political activist Ajibade Idowu said.

Since independence from Britain in 1960, Africa's most populous nation has spent less than 10 years under civilian rule. Last year military ruler General Sani Abacha said he would hand over to an elected government by October 1998.

The 15 aspiring parties were told they each had to have well over a million members, with 40,000 from each of Nigeria's 30 states, as well as offices and staff. But these were apparently not fully binding conditions.

"Not less than 50 percent (of conditions) is regarded as the basic qualification for registration," said NECON chairman Sumner Dagogo-Jack as he announced the names of the qualifiers in the capital Abuja.
On Monday Abacha laid the foundation stone for a new 5.46 billion naira ($68 million) parliament building that will house an elected national assembly.
"This is the practical demonstration to show that our transition programme is on course," he said.
Nigerian opposition groups and Western governments, demanding Abacha hand over power earlier, remain unimpressed with the transition programme.
Abacha's government is seen as a pariah by much of the international community after it executed nine minority rights activists in November but insists it will follow its own course to democracy.

The Commonwealth, a grouping of Britain and its former colonies and protectorates, suspended Nigeria last November after the executions but on Sunday decided not to apply sanctions and to maintain dialogue with the oil-rich state.
The eight-nation Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group, meeting in New York, dropped a demand that its planned fact-finding mission to Nigeria be allowed to meet opposition and human rights groups.
The five parties qualifying for registration were headed by the United Nigeria Congress Party of Yahaya Gusau, a veteran conservative from the North who frowns on radical change.
Also successful was the National Centre Party of Nigeria, led by former oil minister Don Etiebet from a minority ethnic group in the oil-producing southeast.
Other qualifiers were the Committee for National Consensus, the Democratic Party of Nigeria and the Grassroot Democratic Movement.
But among those which failed to win registration were the People's Progressive Party, largely made up of opponents of the military from the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO).

NADECO, with its southwestern heartland, has campaigned for Abacha to respect the results of presidential elections in 1993 which millionaire businessman Mashood Abiola is widely believed to have won.
